transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Well, Doc, it's... it's kind of a long story, but I'll try to give you the background so it makes sense. You see, I run my own company. Built it from the ground up, actually, which is something I take a lot of pride in, especially since I didn't even finish high school. The traditional classroom just wasn't built for a guy like me, but out in the real world, I made it work. Anyway, I'm the chief executive now, so as you can imagine, I've got a massive amount on my plate on any given day. A lot of moving parts, a lot of employees depending on me to steer the ship. 

But what actually made me come in today—and I actually had my assistant book this appointment because I knew I'd just keep putting it off—is that for the past year or so... man, it's just getting ridiculous. It's like my filter is completely gone. The absolute smallest thing will just completely derail me. 

I'm talking about, like, my phone will give a tiny buzz on the desk—not even a ring, just a quick vibration—or somebody will just walk past the glass outside my office door. Or, honestly, I'll just be sitting there looking at a budget report and a completely random thought about my in-laws will pop into my head. Like, what my father-in-law said at a barbecue three months ago, or whether we're supposed to visit them this weekend. And before I can even stop myself, before my brain can even say "hey, focus," I'm completely pulled off what I'm doing. I'm down some mental rabbit hole, or I'm up out of my chair seeing who just walked down the hall. It's just... it's been a solid year of this, and it's driving me absolutely up the wall because I have a company to run, you know? I can't be getting hijacked by every little stray thought or shadow in the hallway.
Have you noticed these issues with distraction and losing focus in other parts of your life, like at home, in conversations, or while driving, or is it mostly when you're at work?

Well, see, that's the thing. It's not just the little distractions pulling me away, it's... it's also when I'm actually trying to stay locked in on something. And to answer your question, yeah, it happens everywhere, but it's really obvious at work because of the stakes, you know? Like, take a planning document, for example. I'll sit down to review our quarterly projections, and I'm good for the first, I don't know, three or four minutes. I'm reading the numbers, I'm analyzing the trends, I'm thinking about our market share. But then... it's like a fog just rolls in. I'm still looking at the page, my eyes are moving over the words, but nothing is sticking. I'm not absorbing a single piece of information. 

And it's even worse when I'm in a meeting. I'll sit down with one of my regional managers—great guy, by the way, brilliant with logistics, I hired him away from a competitor two years ago—and we'll be discussing the supply chain issues we've been having. And I start off strong! I'm nodding, I'm engaged, I'm making eye contact. But pretty soon, maybe five minutes in, I'll suddenly snap back to reality and realize I have absolutely no idea what he just said for the last two minutes. I'll have to stop him and say, "Hey, sorry, I missed that last part, can you run it back?" And I have to do that all the time. It's embarrassing, frankly. I'm the CEO, I'm supposed to be the one with the sharpest mind in the room, and I'm constantly asking people to repeat themselves because I just... drift off. It happens with my wife too, honestly. She'll be telling me about her day or what we need to do for the kids' school fundraiser, and I just lose the thread completely. It's like my brain just refuses to hold onto one thing for more than a few minutes at a time.
Do you find yourself feeling restless, fidgety, or unusually active, especially in situations where you're expected to stay still, like during meetings or while driving?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, sitting still? That’s... that's practically torture for me sometimes. It’s funny you mention meetings because that’s exactly where it hits the hardest. We have this big, heavy mahogany conference table in the boardroom—gorgeous piece of furniture, actually, I had it custom-made by this local woodworker when we expanded into the new office space last year, really impressive stuff—but sitting around it for more than ten minutes? I just can't stay planted. 

I’m usually bouncing my knee up and down under the table. Like, constantly. Or I’ll grab whatever is in front of me, usually a pen, and I don't even realize I'm doing it at first, but I'll just be clicking it. Click, click, click. Or I'm constantly shifting around in the chair, crossing one leg, then the other, leaning forward, leaning back, adjusting my posture. And the thing is, I'm genuinely trying to listen to my team! I want to hear what they have to say. But lately, I've noticed people... well, they've started giving me these looks. 

Like my VP of Sales, for instance. She was giving a presentation on Tuesday, and she just stopped talking and looked at me because she thought I was getting impatient. People are giving me these looks like I’m rushing them, like I'm trying to say "wrap it up, let's go," even when I’m honestly just trying to listen and absorb what they're saying. She actually asked me, "Am I taking up too much of your time?" And I had to backtrack and say, "No, no, I'm just... I just have a lot of energy today." But it's not just that day, it's every meeting. It's like my body just has to be doing *something* physically, even if my brain is trying to focus on the numbers on the screen. And I know it looks unprofessional for the head of the company to be squirming around, but I just can't seem to stop the physical restlessness, you know? It's like I have a motor running inside me that just doesn't have an off switch.
Have you found yourself interrupting people more often than usual, having trouble waiting your turn, or talking excessively, even when it might not be appropriate?

Yeah, that is... that is actually a real sore spot lately. I didn't even realize how bad it was getting until recently, but I have definitely been cutting people off way more than usual. It is like I just cannot hit the brakes on my mouth. 

Take work, for example. I am constantly finishing my employees' thoughts before they are even done speaking. Just the other day, I was talking with my operations director—great guy, really thorough, maybe a little too thorough sometimes, which is probably why I get antsy—but he was trying to explain this new safety protocol for the warehouse floor. And before he could even get the main idea out, I just jumped right in and finished his sentence for him and immediately moved on to the next topic. I could literally see his face just drop. I can tell it really rubs people the wrong way, because it makes them feel like I am dismissing them or I think I don't need their input. But it is not that at all, my brain is just already three steps ahead and I just blurt it out before I can stop myself.

And it is happening at home, too, which is honestly causing some real friction with my wife. Like, she will be talking to her parents—whether she is on the phone with them or we are over at their place for Sunday dinner, they live about forty minutes away in this nice little suburb so we see them pretty often—and she will be in the middle of telling them a story. Maybe about the kids, or something that happened during her week, and I will just completely jump into her conversation. I will just hijack it, take over the story, or cut her off to add my own two cents. She actually pulled me aside last weekend to tell me how disrespectful it felt. 

And I felt terrible, I really did, because I am not trying to be a jerk. I just get this overwhelming urge to push the conversation forward, or I am so eager to get my thought out before I forget it that I just bulldoze right over whoever is talking. But yeah, the interrupting is definitely a big problem right now, and I know it is wearing thin on the people around me.
Looking back, did you have similar issues with focus, restlessness, or interrupting others when you were a child, or did these problems start more recently as an adult?

Well, you know, I’ve actually been thinking a lot about that lately, trying to figure out if the stress of running the company just finally broke my brain or if it's always been this way. And honestly? Looking back... no, this isn't a new thing at all. This was absolutely around when I was a kid, too. 

I mean, school was... well, let's just say a traditional classroom environment and I were never really a great match, which is probably why I ended up taking my own path and jumping into business early on instead of finishing things out the normal way. But back in elementary and middle school, I was exactly like this. I remember my teachers were constantly—and I mean *constantly*—moving my seat. It was almost like a running joke. I’d start the year somewhere in the middle or the back of the room, and by October, I was parked right up front, usually right next to the teacher's desk. 

Like Mrs. Gable in fifth grade, for example. She had this little wooden desk right up by the chalkboard, and she made me sit right next to it because I just talked way too much to whoever was sitting next to me. I couldn't help it, if a thought came into my head, I had to share it with my neighbor. And if I wasn't talking, I was just getting up out of my chair without asking. I’d wander over to the pencil sharpener, or go look at the class pet, or just stand up because my legs felt like they were vibrating and I couldn't bear to be sitting down anymore. 

And the interrupting? Oh, man, that was there too. The teachers would be halfway through asking a question to the class, and I wouldn't even raise my hand, I’d just blurt out the answer before they could even finish the sentence. I remember getting in so much trouble for it, because they thought I was being a smart aleck or trying to show off, you know? But I really wasn't! I just... the thought popped into my head and my mouth opened before my brain could tell it to wait its turn. So, yeah, to answer your question, it’s not just a recent adult thing. It’s been happening for as long as I can remember, really. It just feels like it has much bigger consequences now that I'm running a company instead of just sitting in Mrs. Gable's math class.
